question: Scattering of α-particles by a thin gold foil suggests the presence of
opt_c: positively charged nucleus at the centre of an atom
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, positively charged nucleus at the centre of an atom. Rutherford fired fast alpha particles (doubly charged helium ions of mass 4 u) at a gold foil about a thousand atoms thick. He expected them all to punch through a soft, evenly spread positive pudding with at most a slight wobble. Most did pass straight through. A few came off at small angles, and roughly one in twelve thousand bounced back the way it had come. Only one arrangement of matter explains that last group. To turn a heavy, fast, positively charged projectile around, the atom must carry a repelling charge that is positive and packed into a tiny volume, and that volume must also hold nearly all the atom's mass. Rutherford named this centre the nucleus .

question: The elements of which of the following pairs are isobars?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, 40¹⁸Ar and 40²⁰Ca. Isobars are atoms of different elements that share a mass number while differing in atomic number. Argon has 18 protons and calcium 20, so they are different elements, yet both nuclides carry 40 nucleons in total. This is the pair NCERT uses to introduce the word, noting that 'the number of protons in these atoms is different, but the mass number of both these elements is 40'. The other three pairs keep the atomic number fixed and change the mass number, which is the definition of isotopes .

question: Which one of the following chemical reactions is not feasible?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, Cu + PbCl₂ → CuCl₂ + Pb. A displacement reaction only runs when the free metal is more reactive than the metal locked in the salt. Read the four lines against the activity series: potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron, lead, hydrogen, copper, mercury, silver, gold, in falling order of reactivity. Iron, zinc and magnesium all stand above copper, so each of them can turn copper out of copper sulphate and take its place. Copper, however, stands below lead. It cannot displace lead from lead chloride, and this reaction simply does not happen.

question: A solution having pH equal to zero is known as
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, highly acidic solution. The pH scale runs from 0 at one end to 14 at the other, and NCERT labels the ends plainly: 0 is very acidic and 14 very alkaline, with 7 in the middle for a neutral solution. pH is a measure of hydronium ion concentration, and the higher that concentration, the lower the pH, so zero is not the absence of acidity but the extreme of it. A solution at pH 0 holds hydronium ions at about 1 mole per litre, which is roughly what you get from concentrated hydrochloric acid.

question: Which one of the following acids is produced in human stomach?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, Hydrochloric acid. The gastric glands in the stomach wall release three things: hydrochloric acid, the protein-splitting enzyme pepsin, and mucus. The acid does two jobs. It creates the strongly acidic medium in which pepsin can work at all, and it kills much of what arrives with the food. Mucus is what keeps the acid from digesting the stomach lining itself; when that balance tips, the result is the pain we call acidity, and the remedy is a mild base such as magnesium hydroxide.

question: Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below the Lists : List-I (Compound) A. Boric acid B. Citric acid C. Magnesium hydroxide D. Acetic acid List-II (Use) 1. Antiseptic 2. Food preservative 3. Antacid 4. Pickle
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, A-1 B-2 C-3 D-4. Take the two easy pairs first. Magnesium hydroxide is milk of magnesia, the mild base NCERT names as the standard antacid for indigestion, so C goes to 3. Acetic acid is the acid of vinegar, and NCERT's carbon chapter records that a 5 to 8 per cent solution of acetic acid in water is called vinegar and is used widely as a preservative in pickles, so D goes to 4. That leaves boric acid and citric acid for antiseptic and food preservative. Boric acid is a long-standing mild antiseptic for minor cuts and burns and the active ingredient of boracic lint, so A goes to 1, and citric acid (used across the food industry as an acidifier, flavouring and preservative, carrying the food-additive number E330) takes 2.

question: The property of the sound waves that determines the pitch of the sound is its
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, frequency. Pitch is how the brain interprets the frequency of a sound: NCERT puts it in exactly those words, and adds that the faster the source vibrates, the higher the frequency and the higher the pitch. A high-pitched sound is one whose compressions and rarefactions arrive at your ear more often per second. The other three quantities on the list describe the same wave but answer different questions: amplitude and intensity govern how loud it seems, and wavelength is fixed once frequency is fixed, because in a given medium the speed of sound is set and wavelength is speed divided by frequency.

question: Which one of the following is not a property of the X-rays?
opt_a: They are deflected by electric fields.
opt_b: They are not deflected by magnetic fields.
opt_c: They have high penetration length in matter.
opt_d: Their wavelength is much smaller than that of visible light.
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, They are deflected by electric fields. X-rays are electromagnetic radiation, and electromagnetic radiation carries no electric charge. An electric field acts on charge, so it has nothing to grip; the same argument covers magnetic fields, which is why statement (b) is a true property and not the answer. This is the standard way of telling X-rays apart from beta rays and alpha rays, which are charged particles and do bend in both kinds of field. Statements (c) and (d) are also true: X-rays run from about 10 nanometres down to 10 picometres in wavelength, far shorter than visible light's 400 to 700 nanometres, and their penetrating power is what makes radiography possible.

question: Which one of the following is not true about the image formed by a plane mirror?
opt_a: It is of the same size as the subject.
opt_d: It is formed as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, It is real image. NCERT's summary of the plane mirror says the image is always virtual and erect, of the same size as the object, as far behind the mirror as the object is in front, and laterally inverted. Options (a), (b) and (d) are three of those four, and all are true. The claim that the image is real is false. Rays from a plane mirror diverge after reflection and never actually meet; they only appear to come from a point behind the mirror, where no light reaches. An image at a place light cannot reach cannot be caught on a screen, and that is what virtual means.

question: In a periscope, the two plane mirrors are kept
opt_c: at an angle of 60° with each other
opt_d: at an angle of 45° with each other
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, parallel to each other. A simple periscope is a tube with a plane mirror at each end, and each mirror is tilted at 45 degrees to the axis of the tube. Light from the scene strikes the top mirror, turns through 90 degrees, runs down the tube, meets the bottom mirror and turns through 90 degrees again into the observer's eye. Two turns of 90 degrees in opposite senses bring the ray back to its original direction, and that only works if the two mirror surfaces are parallel to each other. The 45 degrees in the design describes each mirror's tilt against the tube, not the angle between the two mirrors, which is zero.

question: If the speed of light in air is 3 × 10⁸ m/s, then the speed of light in a medium of refractive index 3/2 is
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, 2 × 10⁸ m/s. The refractive index of a medium is the speed of light in air divided by the speed of light in that medium. Rearranged, the speed in the medium is the speed in air divided by the refractive index. Here that is 3 × 10⁸ divided by 3/2, which is 3 × 10⁸ multiplied by 2/3, giving 2 × 10⁸ metres per second. The sense of the result is a check in itself: a refractive index greater than one means light is slower in the medium than in air, so the answer must be smaller than 3 × 10⁸, and 2 × 10⁸ is. This is NCERT's own exercise, which asks for the speed of light in glass of refractive index 1.50 given a vacuum speed of 3 × 10⁸ metres per second, with 1.50 written here as a fraction.

question: Which one of the following types of radiation has the shortest wavelength?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, Ultraviolet (UV). Arrange the four by wavelength and the order is fixed: radio waves are the longest, running from millimetres to kilometres; infrared comes next, roughly 700 nanometres up to a millimetre; visible light occupies about 400 to 700 nanometres; ultraviolet lies just beyond the violet end at 100 to 400 nanometres. Ultraviolet is the only one of the four shorter than visible light, so it has the shortest wavelength and, correspondingly, the highest photon energy of the group.

question: The unit of the force constant k of a spring is
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, N/m. The force constant of a spring comes from Hooke's law, which says the restoring force is proportional to the extension: F equals k times x. Rearranged, k equals F divided by x, so its unit is the unit of force divided by the unit of length: newton per metre. Read physically, k is the force needed to stretch or compress the spring by one metre, so a stiff spring has a large k and a slack one a small k. Every unit question of this kind is settled the same way: write the defining equation, make the wanted quantity the subject, and substitute units for symbols.

question: Which one of the following is not an epidemic disease?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, Elephantiasis. An epidemic is a rapid rise of a disease to a large number of cases in a population within a short period. Cholera, malaria and smallpox all behave that way: cholera flares after floods and in crowded camps, malaria surges in transmission seasons and after population movement, and smallpox spread explosively from person to person until vaccination stopped it. Elephantiasis does not. It is the late, disfiguring swelling of lymphatic filariasis . It builds only after repeated infected mosquito bites over months or years, with the worms taking about a year to mature and then living five to eight years. A condition that needs years of repeated exposure in one place cannot produce the short, sharp curve of an epidemic. It is endemic instead, held at a steady level wherever the vector and the parasite persist.

question: Which one of the following animals has a three-chambered heart?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, Salamander. Heart chambers track how an animal manages its body temperature. Amphibians and most reptiles have three-chambered hearts (two atria and a single ventricle) and tolerate some mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood, because they do not spend energy keeping their body warm. A salamander is an amphibian, so three chambers is exactly right. Fishes have two chambers, and blood passes through the heart once per circuit. Birds and mammals, which burn energy constantly to hold their temperature steady, need fully separated streams and so have four chambers.

question: Which one of the following is the correct sequence of events during sexual reproduction in plants?
opt_a: Seedling, formation of embryo, pollination, fertilization, division of zygote
opt_b: Formation of embryo, seedling, pollination, fertilization, division of zygote
opt_c: Pollination, fertilization, division of zygote, formation of embryo, seedling
opt_d: Seedling, formation of embryo, division of zygote, pollination, fertilization
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, Pollination, fertilization, division of zygote, formation of embryo, seedling. The order follows the plant's own logic. Pollen has to reach the stigma first, and that transfer is pollination. A tube then grows from the pollen grain down through the style to the ovule, where the male germ cell fuses with the egg (fertilisation) and the fusion produces the zygote. The zygote divides repeatedly to form an embryo inside the ovule, the ovule hardens into a seed and the ovary ripens into a fruit. Only when the seed germinates under suitable conditions does the embryo grow into a seedling. Nothing can be shuffled: no fertilisation without pollination, no zygote without fertilisation, no embryo without a dividing zygote, and no seedling without an embryo.

question: When air is blown from mouth into a test tube containing limewater, the limewater turns milky. This is due to the presence of
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, carbon dioxide. Limewater is a solution of calcium hydroxide, and carbon dioxide turns it milky by forming a white precipitate of calcium carbonate: the reaction NCERT writes as calcium hydroxide in solution plus carbon dioxide gas giving solid calcium carbonate and water. Exhaled air carries roughly four per cent carbon dioxide against the 0.04 per cent in ordinary air, which is more than enough to cloud the solution in seconds. That is why blowing through a straw into limewater is the standard classroom demonstration that respiration releases carbon dioxide. Keep bubbling gas through and the milkiness clears again as the insoluble carbonate turns into soluble calcium hydrogencarbonate.

question: Which one of the following is the ‘energy currency’ for cellular processes?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, ATP. The phrase in the question is lifted from NCERT, which states that ATP is the energy currency for most cellular processes. Respiration breaks glucose down and the energy released is used at once to build ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate. Cells then spend that ATP wherever work is needed (muscle contraction, protein synthesis, nerve impulses) by breaking the terminal phosphate linkage, which releases about 30.5 kilojoules per mole. The comparison NCERT draws is with a battery: one store of energy that can be drawn on for many different kinds of task.

question: Which one of the following is the first enzyme to mix with food in the digestive tract?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, Amylase. Digestion begins in the mouth, before food has gone anywhere else. Saliva from the salivary glands contains salivary amylase, which starts breaking starch down into simpler sugars while the tongue mixes the food. Anything secreted further along the canal necessarily meets the food later: pepsin waits in the stomach and trypsin further on in the small intestine. So the first enzyme to mix with food in the digestive tract is amylase, and the reason is anatomical order rather than any property of the enzyme itself.

question: Mahatma Gandhi’s Dandi March, a great event in Indian freedom struggle, was associated with
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, sodium chloride. The Dandi March was a protest against the British salt monopoly and the tax it carried, and common salt is sodium chloride. Gandhi left Sabarmati Ashram on 12 March 1930 with 78 volunteers and walked about 385 kilometres to the coastal village of Dandi in Gujarat, reaching it on 5 April. At half past eight on the morning of 6 April he picked up natural salt from the shore and broke the Salt Act of 1882. The choice of salt was deliberate: it was a necessity every household bought, rich and poor alike, so a tax on it touched everyone and the law could be broken by anyone who walked to the sea.

question: Match List–I with List–II and select the correct answer using the code given below the Lists: List–I (Name) A. Bleaching powder B. Baking soda C. Washing soda D. Slaked lime List–II (Formula) 1. NaHCO₃ 2. Na₂CO₃·10H₂O 3. Ca(OH)₂ 4. CaOCl₂
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, A B C D 4 1 2 3. Take the formulae one at a time. Bleaching powder is written CaOCl₂ and is made by passing chlorine over dry slaked lime, so A goes to 4. Baking soda is sodium hydrogencarbonate, NaHCO₃, so B goes to 1. Washing soda is Na₂CO₃·10H₂O (sodium carbonate with ten water molecules of crystallisation) so C goes to 2. Slaked lime is calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)₂, the base that limewater is made from and that bleaching powder is made out of, so D goes to 3. That is 4, 1, 2, 3 in order.

question: The number of water molecules associated with copper sulphate molecule to form crystals is
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, 5. Hydrated copper sulphate is CuSO₄·5H₂O, and NCERT puts it plainly: five water molecules are present in one formula unit of copper sulphate. Those five are the water of crystallisation, a fixed number of water molecules built into the crystal rather than moisture clinging to its surface, which is why the dry blue crystals do not feel wet. Heat them and the water is driven off, leaving anhydrous copper sulphate, which is white; add water back and the colour returns. That reversible change is itself the classic school test for the presence of water.

question: Silver articles become black after some time when exposed to air because
opt_a: silver gets oxidized to silver oxide
opt_b: silver reacts with moist carbon dioxide in the air to form silver carbonate
opt_c: silver reacts with sulphur in the air to form a coating of silver sulphide
opt_d: silver reacts with nitrogen oxides in the air to form silver nitrate
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, silver reacts with sulphur in the air to form a coating of silver sulphide. The stem and this option are NCERT's own sentences on corrosion, almost word for word: silver articles become black after some time when exposed to air, because the metal reacts with sulphur in the air to form a coating of silver sulphide. The compound is Ag₂S, a dense black solid, and the sulphur reaching the metal is mainly traces of hydrogen sulphide in the atmosphere. The film is thin and self-limiting, which is why tarnish dulls silverware without eating it away.

question: If x is the temperature of a system in Kelvin and y is the temperature of the system in °C, then the correct relation between them is
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, x = 273 + y. The Kelvin and Celsius scales are graded in steps of the same size (a rise of one kelvin and a rise of one degree Celsius are the same amount of warming) but their zeros sit in different places. Absolute zero, 0 K, is −273.15 °C, so the Kelvin reading is always the Celsius reading shifted up by 273.15, rounded in school work to 273. Test it on a familiar pair: water freezes at 0 °C, which is 273 K, and boils at 100 °C, which is 373 K. Both fit x = 273 + y and none of the other three options survive either check.

question: The resistivity ρ of a material may be expressed in units of
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, ohm-cm. Resistivity comes from the relation between resistance, length and cross-sectional area: R equals rho times length divided by area, so rho equals R times area divided by length. Substituting units gives ohm times square centimetre divided by centimetre, which is ohm-centimetre. In SI the same argument gives the ohm-metre, and that is how the quantity is formally defined: a cube of material one metre on a side with a resistance of one ohm between opposite faces has a resistivity of one ohm-metre. Ohm-centimetre is the same quantity in centimetre-gram-second units, and it is still common in materials data.

question: The electromagnetic waves, which are used for satellite communication, are
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, radio waves. A satellite link is a radio link. Communications satellites work across a wide range of radio and microwave frequencies (the C, Ku and Ka bands for civil traffic, UHF, SHF and EHF for military systems) and the microwave bands used for most of that traffic are themselves the short-wavelength end of the radio spectrum. The physical reason radio is the right choice is that these wavelengths pass through the atmosphere and through cloud with little absorption, and can be focused by a dish of practical size. The whole point of putting a relay in orbit is that terrestrial radio links travel by line of sight and are blocked by the curve of the Earth; the satellite carries the signal over that curve.

question: Which one of the following is the correct sequence of organs that occur in the path of urine flow in human body?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, Kidney, ureter, urinary bladder, urethra. The human excretory system is a pair of kidneys, a pair of ureters, a urinary bladder and a urethra, and urine moves through them in that order. NCERT puts it in one sentence: urine produced in the kidneys passes through the ureters into the urinary bladder, where it is stored until it is released through the urethra. Filtration happens in the nephrons of the kidney, so the kidney has to come first; the bladder is the store, so it must sit between the tubes that fill it and the tube that empties it; and the urethra is the single exit, so it must come last.

question: Which of the following endocrine glands is not found in pair in humans?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, Pituitary. The pituitary is a single gland on the midline. It hangs from the base of the brain below the hypothalamus and sits in the sella turcica, a hollow in the sphenoid bone, and it is roughly the size and shape of a kidney bean, about a centimetre across. The other three glands on the list come in pairs, because they are bilateral organs. The adrenals sit one above each kidney, and the gonads (testes in males and ovaries in females) are a pair in each case. So the pituitary is the only unpaired gland named here.

question: Which one of the following cell organelles contains DNA?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, Mitochondrion. Most of a cell's DNA is in the nucleus, but the mitochondrion carries a small genome of its own: in humans a circular molecule of 16,569 base pairs coding for 13 proteins, all of them subunits of the oxidative phosphorylation machinery. It also has its own ribosomes and makes some of its own protein. The reason is evolutionary: mitochondria descend from bacteria engulfed by the ancestors of modern cells, and the endosymbiotic theory explains the retained circular genome as a relic of that ancestry. In plant cells the plastids, including chloroplasts, hold DNA for the same reason. The Golgi apparatus, lysosomes and endoplasmic reticulum have none.

question: Who among the following scientists introduced the concept of immunization to the medical world?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, Edward Jenner. Jenner, an English physician, tested the country observation that people who had caught cowpox did not take smallpox. On 14 May 1796 he inoculated James Phipps, the eight-year-old son of his gardener, with matter from cowpox blisters on the hand of a milkmaid, Sarah Nelmes. Phipps developed a fever and nothing more. On 1 July that year Jenner challenged him with smallpox material by the usual method of the time, and no disease followed. Others had tried cowpox before him; his distinct contribution was to prove that those inoculated were then immune, and to show the protection could be passed from person to person. The words vaccine and vaccination come from his term for cowpox, variolae vaccinae, the pustules of the cow.

question: On 31st December, 1929, in which one of the following Congress Sessions was proclamation of Purna Swaraj made?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, Lahore. The Congress met at Lahore in the last week of December 1929 with Jawaharlal Nehru in the chair. There the party abandoned dominion status as its goal and resolved on Purna Swaraj : complete independence. The date the paper fixes on, 31st December 1929, is the night the resolution was made public on the bank of the Ravi, when the tricolour of independence went up at midnight. The session fixed 26 January 1930 as the day to observe as Independence Day. It also asked Congress members to withdraw from the legislatures and authorised the Working Committee to launch civil disobedience: the road that led to the Dandi March three months later.

question: Which one of the following Acts reserved seats for women in Legislatures in accordance with the allocation of seats for different communities?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, The Government of India Act, 1935. This is the statute that first set aside seats for women in Indian legislatures and then distributed those seats across the communal blocks (general, Muslim, Sikh, Indian Christian, Anglo-Indian) into which the electorate had already been divided. The scheme came out of the Second Round Table Conference, which recommended both that each provincial legislature reserve seats for named communities and that about 2.5 per cent of the total seats go to women. The 1935 Act carried that recommendation into law, reserving the women's seats in the lower houses of the provinces while shutting women out of the upper chambers altogether. It also widened the franchise so that roughly six million women could vote, up from a few hundred thousand.

question: Which one among the following was demanded by the All India Depressed Classes Leaders' Conference at Bombay in 1931?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, Separate electorates for untouchables. Through 1931 the leadership of the Depressed Classes, headed by B. R. Ambedkar, pressed one demand above all: that the untouchable castes should elect their own representatives from their own rolls, rather than be chosen by an electorate the caste Hindus dominated. At the Round Table Conferences Ambedkar argued that caste-Hindu reformers could not represent the Depressed Classes, who needed leaders of their own. The demand was conceded a year later: Ramsay MacDonald's Communal Award of 16 August 1932 extended separate electorates to them, reserving seats in the legislatures. Gandhi's fast unto death in Yerwada jail then forced the Poona Pact of 24 September 1932, which kept the seats but put them inside a joint Hindu electorate.

question: Who among the following was one of the founders of the Indian Society of Oriental Art?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, Abanindranath Tagore. The Indian Society of Oriental Art was founded in Calcutta in 1907 by the brothers Gaganendranath and Abanindranath Tagore, with a group of Europeans in the city backing it and Lord Kitchener as its first president. Abanindranath was the moving spirit of what came to be called the Bengal School: he had trained in European academic technique, turned away from it, and looked instead to Mughal and Rajput miniature and to Japanese wash for a way of painting that would be recognisably Indian. The Society gave that project an institution: exhibitions, a journal and a teaching circle out of which Nandalal Bose, Asit Kumar Haldar and Kshitindranath Majumdar came. Art historians classify his work as revivalist for exactly this reason.

question: Who among the following Sultans succeeded in finally breaking and destroying the power of Turkan-i-Chihalgani?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, Balban. The Turkan-i-Chihalgani, the Corps of Forty, was the body of Turkish nobles built up by Iltutmish, and after his death in 1236 it made and unmade sultans for thirty years. Balban knew it from the inside: he had been one of the Forty himself, and had risen through it as naib to the puppet sultan Nasiruddin Mahmud. Once he took the throne in his own name in 1266 he set about destroying it: rivals were poisoned, demoted or sent to distant posts, and their place was taken by a court theory that put the sultan beyond the reach of any noble. He called himself Zil-i-Ilahi, the Shadow of God, claimed descent from the legendary Afrasiyab, and made courtiers perform sijda and paibos. A network of barids reporting only to him watched the rest.

question: Who among the following Mongol leaders/commanders did not cross Indus to attack India?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, Chenghiz Khan. Genghis Khan reached the Indus in 1221 while hunting down Jalal al-Din Mingburnu, the fugitive prince of Khwarazm, and beat him at the Battle of the Indus. Jalal al-Din swam the river and escaped eastwards; Genghis did not follow. He detached two tumens under Dorbei the Fierce and Bala to continue the chase and himself turned back, so the one Mongol name every student knows is the one that never crossed into India. The other three did. Abdullah, a Negudari governor descended from the family of Chagatai, brought a force into the Punjab in 1292 and was beaten by Jalaluddin Khalji. Qutlugh Khwaja, a son of Duwa Khan, marched on Delhi itself in late 1299, was badly wounded at the battle of Kili and died on the way home. Tair Bahadur is likewise recorded among the Mongol commanders who campaigned into India.

question: In the region of eastern shore of Adriatic Sea, a cold and dry wind blowing down from the mountain is known as
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, Bora. The bora is a northerly to north-easterly katabatic wind of the Adriatic: cold, dry and violently gusty, pouring down the Dinaric ranges onto the coasts of Slovenia, Croatia and Montenegro and onto Trieste. Cold dense air ponds over the snow-covered plateaus behind the coast; when it spills over the ridge it warms as it descends, but it starts so cold that it still arrives at sea level as a cold wind. That is the detail the stem is pointing at. Bora gusts have been clocked above 220 km/h, with 248 km/h recorded at the Maslenica Bridge near Zadar, and the wind is commonest in winter.

question: Nyishi tribe is found mainly in
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, Arunachal Pradesh. The Nyishi are the most populous tribe of Arunachal Pradesh, about 249,824 people at the 2011 Census, just ahead of the Adi. They are spread across a broad belt of the state (Kra Daadi, Kurung Kumey, East Kameng, West Kameng, Papum Pare, Keyi Panyor, Lower Subansiri, Kamle and Pakke Kessang) and spill over into Sonitpur and North Lakhimpur districts of Assam. The traditional man's headgear is a cane helmet topped by a hornbill beak, called pudum or padam, and the demand for beaks once told badly on hornbill numbers. Since 2011 the Hornbill Nest Adoption Programme has turned Nyishi men who used to hunt the birds into paid protectors of their nests in the forests around Pakke Tiger Reserve.

question: In the field of tourism, which one of the following Indian States is described as 'One State Many Worlds'?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, Karnataka. 'One State Many Worlds' was the tourism tagline of Karnataka, and the claim behind it is a real one: the state runs from the Konkan beaches through the Western Ghats rainforest to the dry Deccan plateau, and its monuments cover Badami and Aihole, Pattadakal, Belur and Halebidu, Hampi, Bijapur, Srirangapatna and Mysuru. Karnataka holds 507 of India's roughly 3,600 centrally protected monuments, second only to Uttar Pradesh, with another 752 protected by the state's own Directorate of Archaeology and Museums. It was ranked the third most popular state for tourism in 2014. Present-day note: Karnataka Tourism now fronts a different campaign line, 'Raaga, Ruchi, Rachane', so a student meeting this item today will not find the old slogan on the department's home page.

question: The number of people per unit area of arable land is termed as
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, physiological density. Human geography uses three density measures off the same population figure, and they differ only in what goes in the denominator. Arithmetic density divides total population by total land area. Physiological density divides total population by the area of arable land: exactly the ratio the stem describes. Agricultural density divides the farming or rural population by the area of arable land. The point of the second measure is that it says something the first cannot: two countries can share an arithmetic density and be nothing alike if one is mostly cultivable and the other mostly desert or mountain. Egypt is the standard illustration, with a modest arithmetic density and an enormous physiological one, because almost the whole population is packed onto the Nile's floodplain.

question: Which one of the following rivers joins Ganga directly?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, Son. The Son rises on the Amarkantak plateau, close to the source of the Narmada, and runs north-east across Madhya Pradesh, Jharkhand and Bihar to meet the Ganga a little upstream of Patna, near Maner. It is the Ganga's largest southern tributary and the only one of the four named rivers that reaches the Ganga at all. The other three are second-order rivers of the same peninsular block: Chambal, Betwa and Ken all flow north into the Yamuna, and their water reaches the Ganga only when the Yamuna itself joins it at Prayagraj. Amarkantak is worth fixing in memory because two great rivers part there: the Son turning north-east for the Bay of Bengal by way of the Ganga, the Narmada running west to the Arabian Sea.

question: Which one of the following is not a type of commercial agriculture?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, Intensive subsistence agriculture. The textbook split is between subsistence agriculture, where the farming household consumes almost everything it grows, and commercial agriculture, where the crop or the herd is raised for sale. Subsistence farming has two branches: primitive subsistence, which is shifting cultivation, and intensive subsistence, the densely worked smallholdings of monsoon Asia. Intensive subsistence agriculture therefore belongs on the far side of the line from every other option here. Dairy farming, grain farming and livestock ranching are all standard commercial types, along with mixed farming, plantation agriculture, Mediterranean agriculture and market gardening. The word intensive is what makes the option tempting: intensive says how hard the land is worked, not who the produce is grown for.

question: Which one of the following is not a land use category?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, Marginal land. Indian land-use statistics come from the land revenue records, and they run to nine named heads: forests; barren and wastelands; land put to non-agricultural uses; area under permanent pastures and grazing lands; area under miscellaneous tree crops and groves; culturable wasteland; current fallow; fallow other than current fallow; and net area sown. Marginal land is not one of them. It is a real phrase in economic geography, used of land that only just repays cultivation and comes under the plough when pressure on land rises, but it is a description rather than a record head, and no revenue clerk enters anything under it. The other three options map onto the list: forestland to forests, pasture land to permanent pastures and grazing lands, and barren and wasteland to the category of that name.

question: Which one of the following is not an objective of the MGNREGA?
opt_a: Providing up to 100 days of skilled labour in a financial year
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, Providing up to 100 days of skilled labour in a financial year. The Act guarantees at least a hundred days of wage employment in a financial year to every rural household whose adult members volunteer to do UNSKILLED manual work. That single word carries the whole answer. The guarantee is deliberately pitched at work anyone can do, without training or a trade, because it is meant to function as a floor under the rural labour market and to be self-selecting: people who have better-paid options do not turn up for it. Everything else in the option list is genuinely part of the design: durable and productive assets are to be created from the work done, livelihood security is the Act's stated purpose, and at least one-third of the beneficiaries are to be women.

question: Which one of the following statements with regard to the functioning of the Panchayats is not correct?
opt_a: Panchayats may levy, collect and appropriate taxes, duties, tolls, etc.
opt_b: A person who has attained the age of 25 years will be eligible to be a member of a Panchayat.
opt_c: Every Panchayat shall ordinarily continue for five years from the date of its first meeting.
opt_d: A Panchayat reconstituted after premature dissolution shall continue only for the remainder of the full period.
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, A person who has attained the age of 25 years will be eligible to be a member of a Panchayat. The age is twenty-one, not twenty-five. Article 243F disqualifies from a Panchayat anyone disqualified for elections to the State Legislature, and then adds a proviso that saves the young: no person shall be disqualified on the ground that he is less than twenty-five years of age, if he has attained the age of twenty one years. The framers of the Seventy-third Amendment deliberately set the local bar lower than the twenty-five demanded for a Legislative Assembly. The other three statements track Part IX accurately: Article 243H on taxes, Article 243E on the five-year term, and the same article on what a Panchayat gets when it is reconstituted after premature dissolution.

question: Which one of the following is the earliest launched scheme of the Government of India?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana. It was launched on 25 December 2000 by Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee, to give all-weather road connectivity to habitations that had none: above 500 people in the plains and above 250 in hill, desert and tribal areas. The other three are all products of 2014. Saansad Adarsh Gram Yojana was launched on 11 October 2014, the birth anniversary of Jayaprakash Narayan; Deendayal Antyodaya Yojana is the 2014 restructuring that brought the rural and urban livelihoods missions under one name; and Deen Dayal Upadhyaya Grameen Kaushalya Yojana, the placement-linked skilling arm of the rural livelihoods mission, dates from the same year. So a fourteen-year gap separates the answer from its nearest rival.

question: Which of the following statements is not correct regarding the Members of Parliament Local Area Development Scheme (MPLADS)?
opt_a: Members of the Parliament (MPs) sanction, execute and complete works under the scheme.
opt_b: Nominated Members of the Parliament can recommend works for implementation anywhere in the country.
opt_c: The scheme is fully funded by the Government of India.
opt_d: The annual entitlement per MP is ₹5 crore.
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, Members of the Parliament (MPs) sanction, execute and complete works under the scheme. Under MPLADS an MP only recommends works; the District Authority sanctions them, releases the money and gets them executed through an implementing agency. That separation is the design of the scheme, and it is why the funds go from the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation to the district authorities and never to an MP. The other three statements are accurate. Nominated Members of the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha may select works in one or more districts anywhere in the country, the scheme is fully funded by the Government of India, and the entitlement has stood at Rs 5 crore per MP since 2011-12.

question: Saubhagya, a Government of India Scheme, relates to which of the following areas?
opt_b: Providing clean cooking fuel to poor households
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, Achieving universal household electrification. Saubhagya is the shorter name for Pradhan Mantri Sahaj Bijli Har Ghar Yojana, announced in September 2017 by the Ministry of Power to take an electricity connection into every household that still lacked one. The outlay was Rs 16,320 crore, of which Rs 12,320 crore was gross budgetary support. Households identified from the Socio-Economic and Caste Census of 2011 got the connection free; others paid Rs 500, recoverable in instalments with their electricity bills. The original target was December 2018. The scheme was declared closed in March 2022, by which point about 2.82 crore households had been connected. Note the contrast the paper is fishing for: the clean-cooking-fuel scheme is Ujjwala, not Saubhagya.

question: The 'Basel Convention' is aimed at protecting human health and environment against adverse effects of which of the following?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, Hazardous wastes. The treaty's full name says it: the Basel Convention on the Control of Transboundary Movements of Hazardous Wastes and Their Disposal. It was opened for signature on 21 March 1989 and entered into force on 5 May 1992, and its purpose is to cut the movement of hazardous waste between countries and, above all, to stop rich countries shipping it to poorer ones for cheap disposal. It works through prior informed consent: a shipment may not leave without the written agreement of the importing state. As of June 2024 it had 191 parties, with East Timor, Fiji, Haiti, South Sudan and the United States outside. Each of the other three options is a real convention with its own subject, which is what makes the set worth learning together.

question: Which one of the following is the biggest cause of incidence of migration of female persons in India?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, Marriage. In the Census of India every migrant is asked why they moved, and the answers are grouped as work or employment, business, education, marriage, moved after birth, moved with household, and other. For women the pattern is overwhelming and stable across censuses: marriage is the single largest reason, accounting for roughly two of every three female migrants at the 2011 Census. The reason is village exogamy in most of India: a woman customarily marries outside her natal village and moves to her husband's, which registers as a change of usual residence even when the distance is a few kilometres. That is also why so much female migration is short-distance and intra-district, while male migration, dominated by work, runs longer and more often crosses state lines.

question: Which one of the following is not correct about Repo rate?
opt_a: It is the interest rate charged by the Central Bank on overnight loan.
opt_b: It is the interest rate paid by the commercial banks on overnight borrowing.
opt_c: It is the interest rate agreed upon in the loan contract between a commercial bank and the Central Bank.
opt_d: It is the cost of collateral security.
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, It is the cost of collateral security. The repo rate is a price for money, not a price for the security pledged against it. In a repurchase transaction a bank sells government securities to the Reserve Bank and agrees to buy them back a short while later at a slightly higher price. The difference, expressed as an annual rate, is the repo rate. The securities are the collateral , and their own cost (what the bank paid for them, or what they are worth in the market) has nothing to do with the rate. Options (a), (b) and (c) describe the same transaction from three angles: the rate the central bank charges, the rate the commercial bank pays, and the rate written into the agreement between them.

question: The Cash Reserve Ratio refers to
opt_a: the share of Net Demand and Time Liabilities that banks have to hold as liquid assets
opt_b: the share of Net Demand and Time Liabilities that banks have to hold as balances with the RBI
opt_c: the share of Net Demand and Time Liabilities that banks have to hold as part of their cash reserves
opt_d: the ratio of cash holding to reserves of banks
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, the share of Net Demand and Time Liabilities that banks have to hold as balances with the RBI. The cash reserve ratio is fixed under the Reserve Bank of India Act, and its defining feature is where the money sits: in the bank's current account with the Reserve Bank, not in its own vaults and not in securities. No interest is paid on those balances. Two of the wrong options are near-misses built on that single distinction. Holding a share of liabilities as liquid assets (cash, gold and approved securities, kept by the bank itself) is the statutory liquidity ratio, a different instrument under a different statute. Holding it as part of the bank's own cash reserves misses the point that the reserve is with the central bank. When the ratio is raised, banks have less to lend, and credit tightens.

question: In economics, if a diagram has a line passing through the origin and has 45° angle with either axis and it is asserted that along the line X = Y, what is tacitly assumed?
opt_b: Both variables are in the same unit.
opt_c: Both variables are in different units.
opt_d: At least one variable is a pure number.
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, Both variables are in the same unit. The line runs through the origin at forty-five degrees to both axes, so at every point on it the horizontal distance from the origin equals the vertical distance. Reading that as X = Y goes beyond geometry: it says the two measurements are equal as quantities , and a quantity can only equal another if both are measured in the same unit. Suppose X is a length in metres and Y a weight in kilograms. The point six metres, six kilograms lies on the line, but writing six metres equals six kilograms asserts nothing meaningful. Same unit is the tacit assumption the question asks for. A further condition hides underneath it: both axes must also be drawn to the same scale , or the equal-quantity line would not come out at forty-five degrees.

question: Who among the following won the Best Men's Player Award of FIFA Football Awards, 2019?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, Lionel Messi. Messi took The Best FIFA Men's Player award for 2019 with 46 points, ahead of Virgil van Dijk on 38 and Cristiano Ronaldo on 36: a narrow result, and one that came after van Dijk had won the UEFA award for the season and lifted the Champions League with Liverpool. The same 2019 ceremony gave Alisson the goalkeeper's award and Jurgen Klopp the men's coach award, so Liverpool carried off two of the three and lost the third by eight points. Do not confuse this award with the Ballon d'Or, which is run separately by France Football; Messi won that for 2019 as well, but the two are different trophies with different voting bodies.

question: In September 2019, which one of the following travel giants declared itself bankrupt?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, Thomas Cook. The British tour and travel company entered compulsory liquidation in the early hours of 23 September 2019, after talks on a rescue package failed. Roughly 600,000 of its customers were abroad at the time, and the UK Civil Aviation Authority mounted Operation Matterhorn to bring home the British travellers among them: about 150,000 people, flown back on some forty chartered aircraft in what was described as the country's largest peacetime repatriation, larger than the Monarch Airlines operation of 2017. Keep the two numbers apart: 600,000 is the worldwide figure for customers stranded, 150,000 the number repatriated by the British operation.

question: Greta Thunberg, a teenaged environment activist who was in news recently, hails from
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, Sweden. Greta Thunberg is Swedish. She began her school strike for the climate outside the Swedish parliament in Stockholm in August 2018, sitting there with a hand-painted board through the run-up to that year's general election, and the weekly Friday strike that followed spread into the international Fridays for Future movement. By 2019 she had addressed the World Economic Forum at Davos, sailed across the Atlantic rather than fly, and delivered the short, angry speech at the United Nations Climate Action Summit in New York in September 2019 that made her a household name: the appearance the paper is calling recent.

question: Recently the Reserve Bank of India has imposed limitations, initially for a period of six months, on the withdrawal of amount by account holders of which one of the following banks?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, Punjab and Maharashtra Cooperative Bank. On 23 September 2019 the Reserve Bank placed the bank under directions for six months and initially capped withdrawals at Rs 1,000 per account: a limit so tight that it caused public alarm and was raised within days to Rs 10,000, then to Rs 50,000 in November 2019 and to Rs 1,00,000 in June 2020. The reason was a concentration of credit that should never have existed: of a loan book of about Rs 8,300 crore, roughly Rs 6,226 crore, some 73 per cent, had gone to a single borrower group, Housing Development and Infrastructure Limited, and the exposure had been concealed behind dummy accounts for years. The bank was eventually merged into Unity Small Finance Bank on 25 January 2022.

question: Amitabh Bachchan was recently conferred with the prestigious Dada Saheb Phalke Award. Who among the following was the first recipient of the award?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, Devika Rani. The Dada Saheb Phalke Award was instituted in 1969, the centenary year of Dhundiraj Govind Phalke's birth, and its first recipient was Devika Rani, honoured at the 17th National Film Awards and widely called the first lady of Indian cinema. She had trained in London, starred in Karma and Achhut Kanya, and with Himansu Rai ran Bombay Talkies, the studio that gave Ashok Kumar and Dilip Kumar their starts. The award the stem calls recent is Amitabh Bachchan's, made for the year 2018 and presented at the 66th National Film Awards. Every other name here is a genuine recipient, just not the first, which is what makes the question a test of one date rather than of the list.

question: The famous Mughal painting, depicting Jahangir embracing the Safavid king Shah Abbas, was painted by which one of the following Mughal painters?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, Abul Hasan. The painting is the allegory of about 1618 in which Jahangir, standing on a lion, embraces Shah Abbas of Persia, who stands on a lamb, the two of them on a globe with a haloed sun behind. It is the work of Abu'l Hasan, whom Jahangir titled Nadir-uz-Zaman, the Wonder of the Age, in 1618 in a note written on the frontispiece of his own memoirs. The painter's own account is that the picture came out of a dream. What it says is political rather than documentary: the two rulers were rivals over Qandahar and never in fact met, and the composition makes the Mughal much the larger figure, pushing the Safavid to the edge of the world. The picture is in the Freer Gallery of Art in Washington.

question: Which of the following statements about 'Mughal Mansab' system are correct? 1. 'Zat' rank was an indicator of a Mansabdar's position in the imperial hierarchy and the salary of the Mansabdar. 2. 'Sawar' rank indicated the number of horsemen the Mansabdar was required to maintain. 3. In the seventeenth century, Mansabdars holding 1000 or above 'Sawar' rank were designated as nobles (Umara). Select the correct answer using the code given below.
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, 1 and 2 only. Statements 1 and 2 are the standard description of the dual rank. The zat fixed a mansabdar's place in the imperial hierarchy and, through the sanctioned pay schedules, his personal salary; the sawar fixed the cavalry contingent he had to maintain and the money he received for maintaining it. Statement 3 fails on a single word. The threshold for being counted among the nobility, the umara, ran on the ZAT rank, not the sawar: 500 zat under Akbar, and 1,000 zat by the seventeenth century. Precedence among nobles followed the same rule, so that a man rated 4,000 zat and 2,000 sawar outranked one rated 3,000 and 3,000. Swap zat for sawar, as statement 3 does, and the claim is no longer true.

question: Which one of the following pairs is not correctly matched?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, Kuddapah-kar : Rocky wastelands. The other three pairs are the ordinary land classes of the Tamil revenue vocabulary and every one of them is matched right. Nancai (nanjai) is wet land: ground commanded by a river channel or a tank and put under paddy. Puncai (puncai/punjai) is dry land, farmed on the rain alone and sown with millets, groundnut and pulses. Tottakkal is garden land, the small watered plots kept for orchards, plantains and vegetables. Those three words are still printed on Tamil Nadu land records: a patta will describe a survey number as nanjai or punjai to this day. The first pair is the one that does not belong. The word paired with 'rocky wastelands' is not a category in that classification at all, and the Tamil revenue system's own name for uncultivable common waste is poramboke: land that carries no assessment and cannot be sold because it belongs to the government. That is why the key marks (a).

question: Which of the following rulers were identified through matronymics (names derived from that of the mother)?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, Satavahanas. Satavahana kings are named after their mothers, not their fathers, and the inscriptions make it unmistakable. Gautamiputra Satakarni means Satakarni, son of Gautami; Vasishthiputra Pulumavi means Pulumavi, son of Vasishthi. The naming element is the mother's gotra name, and the practice runs through the dynasty rather than appearing once. The most famous Satavahana record is itself a mother's: the Nashik prashasti was commissioned by Gautami Balashri, mother of Gautamiputra, and it is she who sets down his achievements, that he destroyed the Sakas, Yavanas and Pahlavas and restored the glory of the Satavahana line. Note that the naming does not make the succession matrilineal: the throne still passed from father to son. What it shows is the standing of royal mothers in Satavahana practice.

question: Which one of the following statements about the famous text of Panchatantra is correct?
opt_a: It is a philosophical text reflecting the debates of the time and refuting rival positions.
opt_b: It is a text ushering in linguistics as a formal science.
opt_c: It is a text discussing developments in various spheres of natural sciences.
opt_d: It is a text showing through illustration what should and should not be done.
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, It is a text showing through illustration what should and should not be done. The Panchatantra is a Sanskrit collection of animal fables in five books, framed as a course of instruction: a king despairs of his three dull sons and hands them to a teacher who undertakes to make them worldly-wise, and the fables are the teaching. The subject is niti (practical conduct, statecraft, the handling of friends, enemies and money) and it is taught not by argument but by illustration, one story opening inside another so that a maxim is always demonstrated rather than asserted. That is exactly what option (d) describes. The book's travels confirm the character: it was turned into Pahlavi in the sixth century and from there into Arabic as Kalila wa Dimna, and through Persian, Syriac, Greek, Hebrew and Latin it became one of the most widely translated books of the pre-modern world: carried everywhere as a manual of worldly wisdom, not as philosophy or science.

question: Geomorphic factors influencing plant and animal distributions are
opt_c: slope angle, slope aspect and relief
opt_d: slope angle, slope aspect and relative relief
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, slope angle, slope aspect and relief. Biogeography groups the controls on where plants and animals live as climatic, edaphic, biotic and geomorphic . The geomorphic set is the landform set: how steep the ground is, which way it faces, and how much height difference the terrain carries. Slope angle governs how fast water drains and how much soil can stay put. A steep face sheds both, so it supports thin-soiled, drought-tolerant communities, while the gentler footslope collects them. Slope aspect decides how much sun a face receives: in the northern hemisphere a south-facing slope is warmer and drier and a north-facing one cooler and moister. Relief, the height range of the land, creates the altitudinal belts that let temperate species live at low latitudes and puts an alpine zone above a tropical forest on the same mountain.

question: Which one of the following groups of cities does not have Sclerophyll as its natural vegetation cover?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, Las Vegas and Queensland. Sclerophyll is the hard-leaved, evergreen, drought-resisting vegetation of the Mediterranean climate: small, thick, waxy leaves that cut water loss through a hot rainless summer, with evergreen oaks, olive, cork oak and aromatic shrubs as the type plants. Mediterranean climates sit on the western sides of continents, roughly in the 30-45 degree belt of both hemispheres, and the other three pairs each name two such places. The fourth pair breaks the pattern twice. Las Vegas lies inland in the Mojave, a true desert whose natural cover is desert scrub, not sclerophyll. Queensland is not a city at all but a large Australian state on the eastern, not western, side of the continent, running from humid subtropical in the south-east to tropical in the north.

question: Which of the following are warm ocean currents?
opt_b: North Atlantic Drift and Brazil Current
opt_d: West Wind Drift and Falkland Current
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, North Atlantic Drift and Brazil Current. Both are warm. The North Atlantic Drift is the Gulf Stream's continuation across the ocean, carried east by the westerlies towards north-west Europe, and it is the reason ports on the Norwegian coast stay ice-free at latitudes where the Canadian side is frozen. The Brazil Current is a western boundary current of the South Atlantic, flowing polewards down the Brazilian coast until it meets the cold Falkland (Malvinas) Current. The general rule does all the work here: western boundary currents run along the eastern coasts of continents, carry warm water polewards, and are narrow, deep and fast; eastern boundary currents run along the western coasts, carry cold water equatorwards, and are broad, shallow and slow, with upwelling and a coastal desert behind them. Every current in the other three options fails that test in at least one member.

question: In India, how many States/Union Territories have more than two international boundaries?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, 4. Count the units that touch three or more foreign neighbours and four is what you get. West Bengal reaches Nepal in the north-west, Bhutan in the north and Bangladesh along its eastern and southern edge. Sikkim is wedged between Nepal to the west, China to the north and Bhutan to the east. Arunachal Pradesh has Bhutan on the west, China across the McMahon Line to the north and Myanmar to the east. Those three are settled and uncontroversial. The fourth is the Ladakh and Jammu and Kashmir sector. Besides China and Pakistan, India claims a 106 km land boundary with Afghanistan, in territory administered by Pakistan as part of Gilgit-Baltistan and abutting the Wakhan Corridor. On India's own map that stretch falls in the Ladakh sector, which therefore has three foreign neighbours. Every other State stops at two or fewer.

question: In the Hadley cell thermal circulation, air rises up and finally descends at
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, subtropical high-pressure cells. The Hadley cell is the thermally driven overturning of the tropical atmosphere. Intense heating at the equator makes air expand, rise and diverge aloft; as it drifts polewards it cools, loses moisture and becomes denser, and by about 25 to 30 degrees of latitude it sinks. That descending limb is what creates the subtropical high-pressure belt (the horse latitudes) and the sinking air warms by compression, its relative humidity falls, cloud cannot form and the great desert belts of the world sit under it, the Sahara, the Arabian, the Thar, the Kalahari and the Australian interior. From the base of those highs the air returns equatorward as the trade winds, closing the loop. The other three options all name the rising end of the same cell rather than the sinking end, which is the distinction the question is testing.

question: Which one of the following soils is characterized by very high content of organic matter?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, Histosol. Histosols are the organic soils of the USDA soil taxonomy: soils made up mainly of organic material rather than of mineral grains. The formal test is a thickness one: 40 cm or more of organic soil material beginning within 40 cm of the surface, with an organic carbon content of 12 per cent or more by weight under the USDA scheme. They form where water stands long enough to keep oxygen out, so dead plant matter accumulates faster than decay can remove it: bogs, fens, marshes and waterlogged uplands. The three grades of that material give the everyday names: peat where the plant tissue is still recognisable, mucky peat where it is half broken down, and muck where decomposition has gone furthest. None of the other three orders is defined by organic content: they are mineral soils named for a clay behaviour, a frozen layer and a subsurface accumulation.

question: Overseas Indians can exercise franchise in an election to the Lok Sabha under which of the following conditions? 1. They must be citizens of India. 2. Their names must figure in the electoral roll. 3. They must be present in India to vote. Select the correct answer using the code given below.
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, 1, 2 and 3. All three conditions hold together. Citizenship first: the franchise in India belongs to citizens, and an overseas Indian who has taken the nationality of another country loses it, because India does not permit dual citizenship, so a person holding an Overseas Citizen of India card is not an elector at all. Second, the name must be on the electoral roll. Since 2010 an Indian citizen living abroad may be enrolled as an overseas elector in the constituency of the address printed in the passport, and enrolment is what turns eligibility into a vote. Third, and this is where the question earns its marks, the overseas elector has to be there in person. There is no proxy and no postal ballot for this category, so voting means travelling back to the constituency and going to the polling station on poll day: a requirement that makes the right largely theoretical for most expatriates. Since all three statements survive, the answer is the all-of-them option.

question: Which one of the following is not a feature of the Ayushman Bharat Scheme?
opt_a: There is no cap on family size and age.
opt_b: The scheme includes pre- and post-hospitalization expenses.
opt_c: A defined transport allowance per hospitalization will also be paid to the beneficiary.
opt_d: The scheme provides a benefit cover of ₹ 10 lakh per family.
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, The scheme provides a benefit cover of ₹ 10 lakh per family. Ayushman Bharat's insurance arm, Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana , gives a cover of ₹ 5 lakh per family per year for secondary and tertiary hospitalisation. It is a family floater , so the amount is shared across the household rather than given to each member. The figure of ten lakh doubles it and is the planted error. The other three statements are genuine design features. There is no restriction on family size, age or gender; pre- and post-hospitalisation expenses are covered; and a defined transport allowance per hospitalisation is paid to the beneficiary.

question: Which of the following are considered to be the four pillars of human development?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, Equity, productivity, empowerment and sustainability. These four are the standard pillars of the human development approach, as set out in the Human Development Reports and reproduced in the school geography syllabus. Equity means access to opportunity irrespective of gender, caste, income or community: it is about what people can reach, not only what they own. Productivity means human labour made more effective by investing in people, so that growth comes from capability rather than from longer hours. Empowerment means the power to make choices about one's own life, which requires a share in political and economic decisions. Sustainability means that the opportunities available to this generation are available to the next, which covers environmental, financial and human resources alike. The three wrong options each swap one of these for a plausible-sounding intruder (inclusion, gender or labour) and it is the swapped term that gives them away.

question: Which one of the following was added as a fundamental duty through the Constitution (86th Amendment) Act, 2002?
opt_a: To strive towards excellence in individual and collective activity
opt_b: To provide opportunities for education to one’s child between the age of 6 and 14 years
opt_c: To work for the welfare of women and children
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, To provide opportunities for education to one's child between the age of 6 and 14 years. The Constitution (86th Amendment) Act, 2002 added a new clause (k) to Article 51A , imposing on a parent or guardian the duty to provide opportunities for education to a child or ward between six and fourteen years. That clause is the eleventh Fundamental Duty and the only one not added in 1976. The same amendment inserted Article 21A , making free and compulsory education for children aged six to fourteen a fundamental right, and substituted Article 45, so that the State now aims at early childhood care and education below the age of six. The other options either belong to the original ten duties inserted by the 42nd Amendment on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee, or are not duties in that form at all.

question: Which one of the following Articles of the Constitution of India protects a person against double jeopardy?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, Article 20. Article 20 guarantees protection in respect of conviction for offences, and it packs three separate safeguards into one article. Clause (1) bars ex post facto criminal law: no one may be convicted except for breaking a law in force at the time of the act, or given a penalty greater than the one prescribed then. Clause (2) is the double jeopardy rule: no person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once. Clause (3) protects against self-incrimination: an accused cannot be compelled to be a witness against himself. All three run in favour of any person, citizen or not, and none can be suspended even during an emergency, because Article 359 as amended in 1978 keeps Articles 20 and 21 outside the reach of suspension.

question: Consider the following statements about Stone Age in India: 1. Different periods are identified on the basis of the type and technology of stone tools. 2. There are no regional variations in the type and technology of tools in different periods. 3. Stone Age cultures of different periods evolved uniformly in a neat unilinear fashion all over the sub-continent. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, 1 only. Statement 1 states the actual basis of the periodisation. Indian prehistory is divided into Lower, Middle and Upper Palaeolithic, then Mesolithic and Neolithic, and the divisions rest on tool types and the techniques used to make them: heavy core tools such as handaxes and cleavers, then flake tools, then blades and burins, then the tiny microliths of the Mesolithic, then ground and polished stone. Statement 2 reverses the truth. Regional variation is one of the strongest findings of Indian prehistory: the Soanian assemblages of the north-west are dominated by pebble and chopper tools while the peninsular sites carry Acheulean handaxes, and raw material (quartzite here, chert there) shapes what could be made. Statement 3 fails for the same reason. Cultures did not advance in a single neat line across the subcontinent; phases overlap, some regions retain older technologies long after neighbours have moved on, and hunter-gatherer and farming communities lived side by side for centuries. So only the first statement stands.

question: From which one of the following factory sites were limestone and chert blades mass produced and sent to various Harappan settlements in Sindh?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, Sukkur and Rohri Hills. The Rohri hills are a scarp of limestone running south-east of Rohri in Upper Sindh, between the Indus on the west and the Nara on the east, about 40 km long and 16 km wide. The limestone carries nodules of chert , a hard fine-grained silica rock that fractures cleanly and takes a razor edge. The hills are dotted with quarry pits and flaking floors: the debris of blade-making on an industrial scale. Chert blades struck here travelled out to Harappan settlements across Sindh, including Mohenjo-daro, which is why the hills are described as a factory site rather than merely a source.

question: The work Siyar-ul-Mutakherin, which describes the Battle of Plassey, 1757, was written by
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, Ghulam Husain. The Siyar-ul-Mutakherin (the Review of Modern Times) is a Persian history of eighteenth-century India written by Sayyid Ghulam Husain Khan Tabatabai, a well-connected Muslim nobleman of Bihar and Bengal who knew the actors he wrote about. It carries the narrative from the later Mughals through the wars of the Bengal succession, the intrigue at Murshidabad, the Battle of Plassey in 1757 and the establishment of Company power, and it was completed in the 1780s. An English translation appeared from Calcutta in 1790, and the book became one of the most-used indigenous sources for the period precisely because it is written from inside the Indo-Persian political world rather than from a Company factory. Of the other three names, two belong to the political history of the age rather than to its literature, and the fourth belongs to a different century altogether.

question: Who believed that the Russian designs were ‘an imminent peril to the security and tranquility’ of the Indian Empire in 1836?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, Lord Palmerston. In 1836 Palmerston was Britain's Foreign Secretary , an office he held from 1835 to 1841, and the direction of policy towards Russia was his. He distrusted the Russian autocracy on principle and read every Russian move in Asia as a challenge to British power. It was from London, not Calcutta, that the alarm about Russian designs on the approaches to India was sounded loudest. Lord Auckland , who took charge as Governor-General on 4 March 1836, is the tempting alternative because the policy was executed on his watch. But the belief that Russian designs threatened India was a London judgement first, and the key assigns it to the Foreign Secretary, who held that view throughout the decade.

question: The ‘Tattvabodhini Sabha’ was established by
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, Devendranath Tagore in 1839. Debendranath Tagore founded the body on 6 October 1839, first as the Tattvaranjini Sabha and almost immediately renamed the Tattvabodhini Sabha: the association of seekers after truth. Its purpose was to study and propagate the Vedanta of the Upanishads and to give the Brahmo position an intellectual base, and it drew in the ablest young men of Calcutta, several of them from the Derozian circle. In 1843 it began the Tattvabodhini Patrika, edited by Akshay Kumar Datta, which became the most serious Bengali periodical of its day and promoted a systematic study of India's past in the Bengali language. Debendranath had joined the Brahmo Samaj in 1843, and in 1859 the Sabha merged into it, giving the Samaj the organisation and the following that Rammohun Roy's original body had lacked after his death.

question: What was the code name given to the first ever tri-service military exercise between India and USA?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, Tiger Triumph. Tiger Triumph is the amphibious exercise India and the United States hold together, and its first edition, from 13 to 21 November 2019 off Visakhapatnam with a landing phase at Kakinada, was the first tri-service military exercise the two countries had ever conducted: India had until then held tri-service exercises only with Russia. About 1,200 Indian and 500 American personnel took part, and the scenario was humanitarian assistance and disaster relief: putting stores ashore, setting up a field hospital and moving civilians out of a stricken coastal area. Since the exam it has become a regular fixture, with a tabletop edition at Visakhapatnam in October 2022, a third edition from 18 to 30 March 2024 and a fourth from 1 to 13 April 2025 involving about 3,000 personnel. The other three options are invented names built on the same pattern, and picking between them is guesswork unless the real code name is known.

question: ‘Naropa’ is an annual festival of
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, Ladakh. The Naropa festival is held at Hemis in Ladakh, at the largest Buddhist monastery in the region, and it is a twelve-year event, which is why it is often called the Kumbh of the Himalayas. It honours Naropa, the eleventh-century Indian mahasiddha whose Six Yogas are a core practice of the Kagyu lineages, and its central moment is the display of the Six Bone Ornaments associated with him, brought out of the monastery's keeping for the occasion. Hemis itself sits on the bank of the Indus about 45 km from Leh and is the principal seat of the Drukpa Kagyu lineage, which organises the festival. The other three options are all Himalayan or north-eastern states with rich festival calendars of their own, but none of them has any claim on Naropa, whose association is with the Drukpa establishment of Ladakh.

question: Which one of the following is India’s official entry for the Best International Feature Film category in the 92nd Academy Awards?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, Gully Boy. Zoya Akhtar's Gully Boy was chosen in September 2019 as India's official entry for the Best International Feature Film category at the 92nd Academy Awards, the ceremony held in February 2020. The category had been renamed that year from Best Foreign Language Film, and each country may submit exactly one title, chosen by a national selection committee: in India's case a panel constituted by the Film Federation of India. The film did not go further: it was not among the ten shortlisted titles and was not nominated. Of the other three, two are genuine 2019 Indian films that were in contention before the committee and one is not a feature film in the relevant sense at all, which is what makes the set work as a question about the selection rather than about the award.

question: The Global Goalkeeper Award is given by
opt_a: the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation. Goalkeepers is an initiative the Gates Foundation launched in 2017 to press for progress on the Sustainable Development Goals. It hands out a set of Goalkeepers Global Goals Awards each September, timed to the opening of the United Nations General Assembly in New York. The Global Goalkeeper Award is the senior of them, given to a leader for driving progress on the Goals. In 2019 it went to Prime Minister Narendra Modi for the Swachh Bharat Mission's sanitation drive, a decision that was itself publicly contested. The other three options are all real institutions, but none of them runs this award.

question: ‘Gandhi Solar Park’ is located at
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, New York. The Gandhi Solar Park is at the United Nations Headquarters in New York, where Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurated it on 25 September 2019 during the General Assembly session. It is a 50-kilowatt rooftop installation of 193 solar panels (one for each member state of the United Nations) funded by India as a gift to the organisation, and it was timed to the 150th birth anniversary of Mahatma Gandhi. The gesture was made alongside India's other climate messaging of that week at the UN Climate Action Summit. The other three options are places that appear in Indian diplomatic news of roughly the same period, which is what makes them plausible, but none of them hosts this installation.

question: Who among the following was the first to arrive in Africa as traders that eventually led to European colonization of Africa?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, Portuguese. The Portuguese reached the West African coast first and stayed longest. Their voyages down the Atlantic shore through the fifteenth century were driven by gold, pepper and a search for a route to the Indies, and in 1482 they built Elmina Castle on what is now the coast of Ghana: the first trading post on the Gulf of Guinea and still the oldest surviving European building in sub-Saharan Africa. Elmina began as a gold factory and later became a depot in the Atlantic slave trade. That fort is the marker the question is reaching for: a permanent European foothold on African soil, planted by traders, from which territorial control eventually grew. The other three powers followed later. The Dutch took Elmina from the Portuguese only in 1637 and founded Cape Town in 1652, and the oldest modern city founded by Europeans on the continent is that Dutch one: a hundred and seventy years after the Portuguese fort.

question: The College of Military Engineering affiliated to Jawaharlal Nehru University is situated at
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, Pune. The College of Military Engineering stands at Dapodi in the north of Pune, on the highway beside the Khadki cantonment, and it is the training institution of the Indian Army's Corps of Engineers. It is affiliated to Jawaharlal Nehru University for its combat training and its B.Tech and M.Tech degrees, which is the detail the stem uses to identify it. Its history explains the location: it began as the School of Military Engineering at Thomason College in Roorkee in 1943, moved to Dapodi by 1948 after independence, and was upgraded from school to college in November 1951 to match the degree-level engineering courses it had begun to run. The other three options are all places with genuine defence or academic institutions, which is what makes them plausible, but none of them houses this college.

question: Which of the following statements with regard to Coal India Limited (CIL) is/are true? 1. CIL has its headquarters at Kolkata. 2. CIL operates through 82 mining areas spread over twenty provincial States of India. 3. CIL is the single largest coal-producing company in the world. Select the correct answer using the code given below.
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, 1 and 3 only. Statement 1 is right: Coal India Limited is headquartered at Kolkata , at Coal Bhavan in New Town, Rajarhat. Statement 3 is right as well: CIL is the largest coal producer in the world by output, a position it has held for years on the strength of India's demand for thermal coal. Statement 2 fails on the count of states, not of mining areas. CIL operates through 83 mining areas (a figure that shifts by a unit or two between annual reports, so 82 is within the range the company has published), but those areas lie in eight states , not twenty. The company's eight wholly owned subsidiaries have command areas across Jharkhand, West Bengal, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh and Assam.

question: Which one of the following climatic types is found in Central Spain?
